verdict.text: The projection composite is a genuinely stronger input (5.6x home / 2.1x away variance explained vs raw ERA; ERA~proj slope -1.22, r2 0.20; ~97-99% OOF coverage). P1 (projection replaces raw ERA as opponent level) delivers the best sealed margin CRPS of all arms (2.51736 vs C0 2.53856, -0.021 beyond the audit noise band) with derived-ML AUC +0.029 and P(win) SD 0.0409->0.0546 (less compression), and the projection is additive to raw ERA (P2 has the best SP bands and totals ECE). BUT the specific defect this arm-test was built to fix — the lambda-edge SP compression — is NOT closed: the sextile spread ratio stays ~0.38 across every arm including the projection arms (target 1.0), the away-side model still uses only ~18% of the projection signal (vs 24.8% of the raw-ERA signal in C1), and the away-fav derived-ML band gap is essentially unchanged (+3.1pp pooled). The mechanism from 39c865e holds: per-game SP quality (even projection-grade) explains <1% of single-game run variance (R2 0.009), and the regularized Poisson fit still shrinks lambda levels at SP extremes regardless of feature strength. The lambda-compression is not recoverable with derivable SP inputs within the current Poisson-tree architecture.
verdict.next_action: PARTIAL: (1) SP-mismatch pricing stays flag-and-route — the binary moneyline owns it; the derived ML remains a totals-context tool. (2) P1/P2 are a separate margin-quality candidate worth a follow-up gate (sealed CRPS/AUC gains are beyond noise but pooled flat, ECE mixed, sealed n=298): run the full ensemble-style margin walk before any engine adoption. (3) The projection is additive to raw ERA (P2), not redundant — if a future engine change happens, feed both levels.
